title: Find your way home
summary: A handoff is hiding in the filesystem. Follow the evidence.
lesson: A path describes where a file lives. Absolute paths begin at /. Relative paths begin at your current working directory.
Use pwd to locate yourself, ls to inspect a directory, and cat to read a text file. Read before changing anything.
hints: Start with pwd and ls.
Read handoff.txt in your home directory.
Run cat /home/learner/handoff.txt, then cat /var/log/relay.log.
why: An absolute path starts from the root directory, regardless of the current directory.

title: Permission denied
summary: Protect a secret while keeping its owner able to use it.
lesson: Unix permissions are grouped by owner, group and other. Read is 4, write is 2 and execute is 1.
A private configuration file usually needs owner read/write, not execute permission or world-readable access. Broad chmod 777 fixes often create a security defect.
hints: Inspect the file with ls -l.
Owner read plus write is 4 + 2.
Run chmod 600 /home/learner/secret.env.
quiz: Only the owner can read and write
why: 600 gives the owner read/write and gives group/other no permissions.

title: The missing process
summary: The Relay worker stopped. Restore it after reading the failure.
lesson: A service is a long-running process that performs work. Its status and logs are separate pieces of evidence.
A restart can mitigate a failure without explaining it. Inspect the failure first, then verify the recovered service. This browser mission models a service manager, not a full Linux host.
objective: Inspect the service log and restart the relay service.
hints: Read /var/log/relay.log.
Check service relay status.
Use service relay restart, then service relay status.
quiz: What does a successful restart prove?
The root cause is permanently fixed
why: Restarting proves only that the process restarted; root cause and end-to-end health still need investigation.

title: The full log directory
summary: Recover disk space without destroying the audit trail.
lesson: df reports filesystem utilization; du helps locate large directories or files. Check both before deleting data.
A noisy debug log can be truncated after its useful evidence is captured. An audit log may be required for investigation and should remain intact. The lab uses a bounded model of disk usage.
objective: Inspect disk use and truncate /var/log/debug.log, preserving audit.log.
hints: Run df -h and du -h /var/log.
The debug log is large; the audit log is required.
Run truncate -s 0 /var/log/debug.log.
quiz: To preserve useful evidence and required records
why: Space recovery should preserve evidence and respect retention requirements.

title: A pipeline that lies
summary: A failing producer is hidden behind a successful consumer.
lesson: By default, Bash returns the exit status of the last pipeline command. A failed producer can disappear behind a successful consumer.
Enable pipefail to make a pipeline fail when an earlier stage fails. It does not replace explicit handling of expected failures.
objective: Add set -o pipefail or set -euo pipefail before the pipeline.
hints: The final cat succeeds even when the producer fails.
Bash has a pipeline failure option.
Add set -o pipefail on its own line.
quiz: Without pipefail, which status normally wins?
why: Bash normally reports the final command status for a pipeline.

title: Spaces break everything
lesson: The shell performs word splitting on unquoted variable expansions. One filename can accidentally become several arguments.
Quote expansions when you want the value preserved as one argument. Double quotes allow variable expansion; single quotes preserve literal text.
objective: Change the printf argument to "$file" so it prints exactly one path.
hints: The variable contains one filename, not two.
Quote the variable at the point it is expanded.
Use printf "%s\n" "$file".
quiz: One argument containing the full value
why: Double quoting keeps whitespace inside the expanded value from splitting it into separate arguments.

title: Find the noisy client
summary: Turn access-log records into a useful error summary.
lesson: A dictionary maps a key to its current count. A single pass over records makes counting linear in the number of records.
Keep the error definition explicit: status codes of 500 and above count here. Ignore successful requests. Test repeated clients and empty input.
objective: Implement error_counts(records), returning counts of 5xx responses per client.
hints: Start with an empty dictionary.
For each record, check status >= 500.
Use counts[client] = counts.get(client, 0) + 1.
quiz: For n records, a dictionary-counting pass is usually…
why: Each record is processed once; dictionary updates are average constant time.

title: Build an incident summary
summary: Make a small, predictable tool for operational data.
lesson: Separate parsing and calculation from presentation. A pure function is easier to test than a function that reads global state.
Represent an empty dataset deliberately. Return a defined error fraction rather than dividing by zero.
objective: Implement summarize(statuses) returning total, errors and error_rate for 5xx statuses.
hints: Count all inputs and 5xx inputs separately.
Return 0.0 for the empty error rate.
Use a conditional expression for division.
quiz: It makes behavior easier to test
why: Pure calculation can be tested without terminals, files or network dependencies.

title: A retry that never ends
summary: Bound an operation that may keep failing.
lesson: A retry policy needs a limit, retryable error classification and a timeout for each operation. Production clients also need backoff and jitter.
This exercise isolates the attempt limit: retry RuntimeError up to attempts times. Return the first success. Propagate the final error. Reject attempts below one.
objective: Implement retry(operation, attempts). Do not catch unrelated exception types.
hints: Use a bounded loop, not while True.
Re-raise RuntimeError on the final attempt.
Check attempts before invoking the operation.
quiz: What else does production retrying need?
Per-call timeout and a bounded backoff policy
why: Limits alone do not bound wall time if an individual call can hang.

title: The busiest endpoints
summary: Rank incident hotspots with a deterministic tie break.
lesson: A frequency map compresses repeated values into counts. Sorting all unique values costs O(u log u), where u is the number of unique endpoints.
A heap can improve top-k selection when k is small. Start with correctness: higher counts first, alphabetically smaller endpoint first for ties.
objective: Return the top k endpoint names from top_endpoints(paths, k). Return [] when k <= 0.
hints: Count paths before ranking.
Sort keys by (-count, endpoint).
Slice the sorted endpoints to k after checking k <= 0.
quiz: What is u in O(n + u log u)?
why: Counting costs O(n); sorting the unique keys costs O(u log u).
tests:
assert top_endpoints([],3) == []
assert top_endpoints(['/a','/b','/b','/a','/c'],2) == ['/a','/b']
assert top_endpoints(['/a'],0) == []
assert top_endpoints(['/z','/z','/a'],1) == ['/z']
solution:
from collections import Counter
def top_endpoints(paths, k):
    if k <= 0: return []
    counts = Counter(paths)
    return sorted(counts, key=lambda x: (-counts[x],x))[:k]

title: Catch the boundary bug
summary: Repair a small implementation by reasoning about edge cases.
lesson: Boundary cases often expose faulty assumptions: empty input, one element, all equal values and values at a threshold.
Availability in this mission counts statuses below 500 as successful. The empty dataset has no observed availability, so return None. This is a teaching definition, not a universal SLI.
objective: Repair availability(statuses). Return a fraction or None for no data.
hints: The denominator must include every request.
A 500 response is a failure; a 499 response is not in this definition.
Use sum(s < 500 for s in statuses) / len(statuses).
quiz: What should no observations mean here?
why: No data should not silently become perfect or zero availability.
tests:
assert availability([]) is None
assert availability([499,500]) == 0.5
assert availability([503]) == 0.0
assert availability([200,201]) == 1.0

title: The midnight backup
summary: The backup works in your shell. It fails every night.
lesson: Cron normally runs with a small environment, a different working directory and no interactive shell profile. Be explicit about executables and files.
A system crontab under /etc/cron.d has five schedule fields followed by a user and the command. A user crontab has no user field. Always capture diagnostics.
objective: Repair the system crontab: run daily at 02:00 as backup, use /usr/bin/python3 and absolute script path, and append both output streams to /var/log/backup.log.
hints: Keep the five schedule fields and the backup user.
Use the interpreter path returned by command -v python3.
Try: 0 2 * * * backup /usr/bin/python3 /opt/relay/backup.py >> /var/log/backup.log 2>&1
quiz: What differs in a system crontab?
It always loads your shell profile
why: /etc/cron.d entries include the execution user after the five schedule fields.

title: The overlapping job
summary: The next job starts before the previous one finishes.
lesson: A schedule controls start times, not concurrency. Long-running jobs may overlap unless the application or scheduler prevents it.
flock can acquire a file lock before executing a command. -n returns instead of waiting when another process holds the lock. A lock is not a replacement for idempotency after crashes.
objective: Wrap the backup with /usr/bin/flock -n /tmp/relay-backup.lock, preserving absolute paths.
hints: The lock should cover the entire backup command.
Use flock -n lock-file command.
Place /usr/bin/flock -n /tmp/relay-backup.lock before /usr/bin/python3.
quiz: Crashes and repeated deliveries still happen
why: A lock controls concurrent execution but cannot guarantee exactly-once effects across failures.

title: The release gate
summary: Do not deploy when a required check is missing or failed.
lesson: A release gate should fail closed: absence of evidence is not success. Use a fixed set of required checks.
This function models the gate shared by a CI pipeline and a local release tool. It is not a GitHub Actions emulator.
objective: Implement can_deploy(checks). Required checks are tests, build and smoke, each exactly True.
hints: Iterate over the required names.
Missing keys must count as failure.
Use all(checks.get(name) is True for name in required).
quiz: If a required check never ran, deployment should…
why: A fail-closed gate requires positive evidence for every required check.
tests:
assert can_deploy({'tests':True,'build':True,'smoke':True}) is True
assert can_deploy({'tests':True,'build':True}) is False
assert can_deploy({'tests':True,'build':False,'smoke':True}) is False
assert can_deploy({'tests':1,'build':True,'smoke':True}) is False
solution:
def can_deploy(checks):
    return all(checks.get(name) is True for name in ('tests','build','smoke'))

title: A reliable handoff
summary: Deduplicate incident events before handing them to the next team.
lesson: At-least-once delivery can send the same event more than once. Idempotent processing avoids repeating side effects.
Preserve the first occurrence of each event ID, maintaining original order. A process-local set is enough for this exercise; production deduplication needs durable state and a retention policy.
objective: Implement deduplicate(events), preserving the first event with each id and the order.
hints: Keep a set of IDs already seen.
Append only the first event for each ID.
Update the set when you append.
quiz: State durability and retention must be designed
why: A restart loses an in-memory set, and unbounded retention eventually exhausts storage.
